analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal fuel-economy standards for cars and light trucks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standards, the federal rules that require automakers to sell cars and trucks whose average fuel efficiency keeps improving. Without the standards, automakers would be free to sell vehicles that use more gasoline, which lowers their engineering and compliance costs but raises what drivers pay at the pump. The bill was introduced by Rep. Roger Williams with one cosponsor and never moved past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Automakers would gain by no longer having to meet rising fuel-efficiency targets, saving on the engineering and compliance costs of building more efficient fleets. Oil refiners and fuel sellers would benefit from higher gasoline demand.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals chapter 329 of title 49, U.S. Code, the federal corporate average fuel economy standards, eliminating the requirement that automakers meet average fuel-efficiency levels for the vehicles they sell.
With the standards gone, vehicle makers would no longer face federal fuel-economy compliance requirements, reducing the cost of producing less-efficient vehicles.

analysis.who_pays: Drivers would pay more at the gas pump over the life of a vehicle, since fuel-efficiency requirements would no longer apply. Americans would also bear more air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions from the fleet of cars and trucks.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the standards would leave drivers buying vehicles that burn more fuel, directly raising their out-of-pocket fuel costs for years after purchase.
The bill removes the main federal lever for reducing gasoline use and vehicle emissions, with no replacement standard offered in the text.

Even some in the auto industry favored keeping uniform national fuel-economy rules rather than a patchwork of state rules, so repeal did not command broad industry agreement; this reflects general reporting rather than the bill file.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes to a narrow set of manufacturers and fuel sellers, while the cost lands on every household that buys a car: higher fuel bills over the vehicle's life and more emissions in the air. The bill offers no consumer protection in exchange, so on balance its effects run against ordinary drivers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams of Texas introduced the bill on March 17, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
A week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill had only one cosponsor, a Republican, and never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the House.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drivers and the public are better off because the repeal never passed, keeping fuel-efficiency standards in place; automakers and fuel sellers gained nothing they sought. The bill's sponsor gained publicity for the repeal effort but no policy change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drivers, since the repeal never passed

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the CAFE standards and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referring the bill to a subcommittee; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor and attracted no Democratic support in the record; it also never generated any recorded votes, so the partisan shape is inferred from sponsorship rather than roll calls.

industries.note: Repealing the CAFE standards would free car and truck makers from federal fuel-efficiency requirements, cutting their compliance costs. Drivers would absorb those savings as higher fuel purchases over each vehicle's life.
A fleet that burns more gasoline means higher fuel sales, so repeal of efficiency standards would raise demand for their product. The public cost is bigger fuel bills and more emissions.
